title: Microplastics in plastic food storage
scope: Tubs, bags, wraps, and containers
description: What studies measured in food wraps and containers, with particle counts, polymer types, size windows, methods, and clear evidence gaps.
body:
Laboratory studies have detected plastic particles released from some food wraps and containers. The amounts depend on the material, liquid, temperature, contact time, and measurement method. These tests do not establish a common release rate for all food-storage products or a measured human health outcome.{{cite:wang-2024-ldpe-food-wrap}}{{cite:wang-2023-polystyrene-containers}}{{cite:cella-2022-food-packaging-methods}}

What this page covers

This page separates food wraps, specific containers, and cooking or ice-cube bags. The reviewed papers include takeaway containers, a limited set of reusable containers, and food films. Direct experiments on ordinary zip-top storage bags and repeated washing/reuse of household tubs are not represented in this selected review. Those gaps remain open; takeaway-box and heat-sealing-film results are not substitutes.

Takeaway and reusable container studies

Direct container studies show why a particle result needs its complete test protocol. Hu and colleagues extracted particles with sequential room-temperature and hot-water flushing. Their combined extract includes readily removable material as well as particles recovered during hot-water treatment. It cannot isolate how much was generated during a single heating event. PP was the dominant identified polymer, with PE and polyester also present. Some particles may have been deposited during manufacture, storage or handling.{{cite:s-cec1e8fa034e}}

Kim and colleagues tested specific disposable and reusable containers with filtered water. Hot-food containers started with water boiled at 100 °C, while other products received room-temperature water. All were gently shaken and held at room temperature for 30 minutes. The reusable group included steel-bodied containers with polymer lids and a PP cup. It was a single-contact comparison, not a trial of repeated household washing and reuse.{{cite:s-928a947ad149}}

Material and experimentPaper-reported resultSize and methodWhat the result means
PP takeaway containers; combined sequential water flushes{{cite:s-cec1e8fa034e}}{{claim:s-cec1e8fa034e-container-range}}Recorded sizes 50–5000 µm; ATR-FTIR of selected particlesObserved sample range; blank-subtracted. Not a single-use release rate or ingested dose.
PP soup container, sample 8; initially boiling water, 30-minute room-temperature hold{{cite:s-928a947ad149}}{{claim:s-928a947ad149-soup-container-8}}20 µm mesh; micro-FTIR mapping and connected-component particle analysisMean ± reported dispersion from triplicate tests; the table does not label dispersion as SD or SE. Identified polymers include PE, PP and PET.

The micro-FTIR paper includes an unidentifiable-particle category in some sample totals. The selected soup-container row has no such unidentifiable particles. Its result is not a representative count for all tubs, all PP products or all meals. The paper's modeled annual intake is omitted here.{{cite:s-928a947ad149}}

A separate whole-filter FTIR paper reported several synthetic polymers and cellulose, but its data-analysis section counted identified pixels as particles. Its abundance estimates are not reproduced in this comparison because that counting definition differs from counting reconstructed physical particles. This is an analytical limitation, rather than evidence that a material releases no particles.{{cite:s-0e7d682e83f6}}

Food-wrap and PS release experiments

A food-wrap study reported particles after cold-storage and heating tests, with results expressed per film area. A separate container experiment used a chemically specific method and reported particles per container. Their different denominators and analytical methods prevent a direct ranking of materials.{{cite:wang-2024-ldpe-food-wrap}}{{cite:wang-2023-polystyrene-containers}}

The listed food-wrap experiments used commercial low-density polyethylene (LDPE) film cut to 6 × 6 cm and immersed in 40 mL ultrapure water, including the cold-storage tests. These are water-contact experiments, not measurements of particles transferred into a meal.{{cite:wang-2024-ldpe-food-wrap}}

This result is not the maximum across all experiments.

The wrap measurements are study-reported point estimates; the inspected main text does not provide numerical uncertainty for each listed count. The source record explains the missing supporting-information review. In the container experiment, the result shown belongs to its pH comparison, rather than an experiment-wide maximum.{{cite:wang-2024-ldpe-food-wrap}}{{cite:wang-2023-polystyrene-containers}}

Bags, wraps, and tubs are distinct

Raman analysis identified polyethylene in experiments on ice-cube bags and emptied rice-cooking bags. Pigment or residual rice material was also present, which shows why visible particles alone do not establish polymer identity. No numerical particle-release rate from those bag experiments is used here.{{cite:cella-2022-food-packaging-methods}}

Another study characterized nanoplastic-sized material from a polypropylene takeaway box and composite heat-sealing films. Its preparation included filtration and further treatment. It does not provide a release count used on this page, and its heat-sealing films do not represent household zip bags.{{cite:wang-2023-nanoplastic-scenarios}}

Screening results need qualification

A preliminary polystyrene-packaging study used Nile Red fluorescence to screen for particulate material. The study separately measured styrene monomer; those chemical concentrations are not particle counts. Individual fluorescent particles were not confirmed by FTIR or Raman in the reported workflow, so its observations should not be combined with chemically identified particle measurements.{{cite:ajaj-2021-polystyrene-packaging}}

How to read the measurements

Look first at the polymer and product tested, then the liquid and contact conditions. Counts normalized to film area do not mean particles per package, and a filtration pore size does not establish the instrument’s detection limit. Sample concentration, drying, cooling, and aggregation can change the particles an analyst observes.{{cite:cella-2022-food-packaging-methods}}

For the wrap study, Nile Red and microscopy supplied the counts; bulk-film FTIR and Raman supplied separate material characterization. For the polystyrene container, µ-FTIR mapping identified particles on the filter. These approaches have different identification strengths and size coverage.{{cite:wang-2024-ldpe-food-wrap}}{{cite:wang-2023-polystyrene-containers}}

Read the testing-method guide →

Regulatory status

FDA describes food-contact authorization in terms of intended use, migration and toxicological evidence. A release count in this page does not determine compliance.{{cite:fda-microplastics-foods}}

The supplied EU restriction concerns specified synthetic polymer microparticles as substances or intentionally present in mixtures. Its scope and exceptions do not turn every particle shed from a container into an automatic violation.{{cite:s-2f1daf6ca78b}}

The cited regulatory sources include drinking-water measurement procedures. Those procedures define analytical methods for their water scope; they do not establish a particle ceiling for food-storage products.{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}}{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}}

Read regulatory scope and source versions →

Common questions

Can the studies give a single count for plastic food storage?

No. The studies test different materials, conditions, denominators, and measurement windows. The results remain separate rather than being combined into one category-wide number.{{cite:wang-2024-ldpe-food-wrap}}{{cite:wang-2023-polystyrene-containers}}

Does a measured particle count establish a health effect?

These release experiments do not measure human clinical outcomes. They cannot establish a disease risk from a particular storage product. The source records state the narrower findings each experiment supports.{{cite:wang-2024-ldpe-food-wrap}}{{cite:wang-2023-polystyrene-containers}}

What can this page say about zip bags and repeated reuse?

The selected review does not establish a numerical release rate for consumer zip-top bags or repeated use of generic household tubs. A single-contact test of a specified reusable container does not answer the repeated-use question. Findings from other container types remain labeled by their actual scope.

What remains uncertain

The available studies do not establish a typical release rate across all food-storage products, an ingested dose per meal, or an equivalent measurement across microplastics and nanoplastics. The wrap study’s full quality-control supplement remains unreviewed. Broader coverage of zip bags, repeated-use tubs, food matrices, and comparable validated methods is needed before those questions can be answered.{{cite:wang-2024-ldpe-food-wrap}}{{cite:cella-2022-food-packaging-methods}}

title: Microplastics in baby wipes
scope: Baby wipes within the broader wet-wipe literature
description: What studies establish about wipe fibers, synthetic polymers, total shedding, and the limits of evidence for infant contact.
body:
Some wet wipes contain synthetic plastic fibers, and laboratory tests show that nonwoven wipes can shed fibers. But a fiber count is not automatically a microplastic count. The reviewed studies include cellulose-based materials, mixed-fiber wipes, and products intended for several uses. They do not establish a typical plastic-particle dose transferred to a baby during wiping.{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}{{cite:s-44cb9cefe164}}

What this page covers

This page places baby wipes in the broader evidence on wet-wipe materials and shedding. The most useful direct studies answer different questions: what the wipe is made of, and what detaches under a specified laboratory challenge. Neither question alone measures how much plastic reaches infant skin, is swallowed, or enters the body. Findings about household or industrial wipes remain labeled by their actual scope.{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}{{cite:s-44cb9cefe164}}

A nonwoven wipe is a bonded web of fibers. Its material can include natural cellulose, regenerated cellulose, polypropylene, polyethylene, or polyester. That mixed composition matters because laboratory instruments can count a cellulose fiber without finding a synthetic plastic polymer. Describing all released fibers as microplastics would change what the study measured.{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}{{cite:s-44cb9cefe164}}

What the studies found

A commercial-wipe study measured material retained after agitation in water and used an optical fiber analyzer to count shed fibers. The table gives source-specific examples that deliberately retain the authors’ different endpoints. The retained mass includes substances other than plastic, and the fiber count is not chemically specific.{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and measurement limits.

Material and studyReported findingMethod and size contextWhat it establishes
Personal-care wipe P1{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}{{claim:s-4b43a51e0282-p1-mass}}Gravimetric retained material after mechanical agitationTotal retained mass; not a plastic mass or infant-contact dose.
Cellulose-based personal-care wipe P2{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}{{claim:s-4b43a51e0282-p2-fibers}}Optical fiber analysis; observed fiber length 0.05-6.15 mmTotal fibers including cellulose; some lengths exceed the usual microplastic size boundary.
Commercial wet-wipe material survey{{cite:s-44cb9cefe164}}Synthetic PP/PET in conventional specimens; cellulose-based fibers in the investigated flushable/biodegradable groupsSEM, ATR-FTIR, evolved-gas MS, pyrolysis GC-MSComposition of tested material, without a particle-release count.

Why test conditions matter

The water-shedding experiment used cut specimens with unsealed edges, metal balls, and controlled agitation. The challenge was designed to represent mechanical stress relevant to disposal and wastewater transport. It was not a simulation of gently wiping skin. Its mass-normalized results cannot be relabeled as particles per wipe used on a child, and its water test cannot supply a dermal absorption rate.{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}

The authors also studied shedding into air with a separate mechanical apparatus. Airborne and waterborne measurements use different collection procedures. A number from one environment should not be used as the other environment’s release rate. The study links shedding behavior to fiber type and bonding, but the products varied in several characteristics, so these findings do not create a universal material ranking.{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}

Composition and shedding are separate measurements

The multi-analytical composition study examined unused wipes after drying. Microscopy described fiber morphology, infrared spectra assessed polymer chemistry, and thermal methods distinguished fibers from organic additives. The conventional specimens included synthetic plastics alongside cellulose, while the selected alternative-material groups were cellulose-based. That result concerns the tested set and does not verify every product carrying a similar label.{{cite:s-44cb9cefe164}}

The same work detected formulation ingredients through separate chemical signals. Additives and dissolved chemicals are not microplastic particles. Detecting an additive does not establish that it came from a released particle, and detecting polymer in a whole wipe does not quantify particle transfer during use. The methods also have limits: drying can remove volatile chemicals, and some ingredients are difficult to resolve by pyrolysis.{{cite:s-44cb9cefe164}}

How strong are the measurements?

The shedding study included water blanks and empty-chamber controls, and it characterized bulk wipe materials. Those steps improve interpretation, but they do not identify the polymer of every fiber counted by the optical analyzer. The waterborne fiber counts were not replicated in the same way as the gravimetric measurements. Retained lotion or detergent affected one specimen’s mass result, illustrating why mass and fiber count can disagree.{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}

The composition study provides complementary chemical identification, but it did not perform the same release experiment. Combining the two studies does not supply missing particle-specific chemistry for the shedding counts. They support a distinction between constituent material, released total fibers, and confirmed released synthetic particles.{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}{{cite:s-44cb9cefe164}}

Regulatory status

The supplied EU restriction concerns defined synthetic polymer microparticles, including applicable intentional uses in cosmetic mixtures. Product type, polymer definition, exemptions and transition provisions must be checked before drawing a legal conclusion.{{cite:s-2f1daf6ca78b}} A paper’s particle count or fiber-shedding experiment alone does not establish compliance. Water-testing procedures in the same folder do not set a particle limit for wipes or cosmetics.{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}} Read the scope and source-version notes.

Cross-contaminant report

Read the published cross-contaminant report on baby wipes for the separate report across contaminant classes. Particle measurements on this page remain tied to the individual papers reviewed here.

What remains uncertain

The reviewed evidence does not establish a typical infant-contact count, a fraction absorbed through skin, or a clinical outcome from baby-wipe use. Broader wet-wipe findings are useful for understanding material composition and possible shedding, but cannot answer those questions by themselves. Comparable tests on intact baby wipes, with realistic wiping conditions and individual-particle chemistry, would address a different and more specific exposure question.{{cite:s-4b43a51e0282}}{{cite:s-44cb9cefe164}}

title: Microplastics in infant feeding bottles
scope: Hot-water release and cap/neck abrasion in selected feeding bottles
description: Raman-identified hot-water release, infrared-confirmed abrasion particles, and why their numbers describe different experiments.
body:
Selected feeding bottles have released plastic particles during hot-water preparation tests and during repeated opening and closing. The results depend on the bottle, handling protocol, particle-size window, and analytical preparation. These studies establish possible release under stated conditions. They do not measure a baby’s internal dose or demonstrate a clinical health effect.{{cite:s-65f1d8743aef}}{{cite:s-80f7cd5b1cac}}

What this page covers

The direct evidence reviewed here separates a water-based simulation of formula preparation from an experiment on cap and neck abrasion. These are distinct sources and denominators. The hot-water experiment reports particles in the collected water. The abrasion experiment reports particles in a concentrated ethanol extract prepared for the instrument. Their numbers cannot be compared as equivalent concentrations in a feed.{{cite:s-65f1d8743aef}}{{cite:s-80f7cd5b1cac}}

The library also contains infant textile and fetal biomonitoring papers. Those do not test feeding-bottle release and are not used as substitutes for bottle measurements. This category is a selected review of direct experimental evidence rather than an exhaustive survey of all bottle designs or feeding practices.

What the studies found

The polypropylene-bottle protocol reports a range of particle concentrations after cleaning, sterilization, and shaking with hot deionized water. Raman measurements identified the polymer in sampled filter regions, and image analysis related the observed regions to the filtered volume. This is a release test in water, without milk powder or a measured amount ingested by an infant.{{cite:s-65f1d8743aef}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and measurement limits.

ExperimentReported resultIdentification and size contextInterpretation
PP bottle preparation protocol{{cite:s-65f1d8743aef}}{{claim:s-65f1d8743aef-bottle-release-range}}Raman in representative filter fields; classification bins begin at 0.8 µmProduct-dependent water-simulant concentrations, with spatial extrapolation.
Cap/neck abrasion in one plastic feeding bottle{{cite:s-80f7cd5b1cac}}{{claim:s-80f7cd5b1cac-feeding-extract-112}}LDIR chemical identification; reported plastic sizes 20-500 µmConcentrated ethanol analytical extract; not a milk concentration.

How the hot-water experiment was done

The protocol cleaned and rinsed new bottles, immersed them in hot water for sterilization, then placed hot deionized water inside and shook the bottle. Glass hardware minimized additional plastic sources. The collection water was filtered, and low-power Raman spectroscopy compared particle spectra with a polypropylene reference. Atomic force microscopy provided separate surface-topography information.{{cite:s-65f1d8743aef}}

Only representative filter regions were examined rather than every point on the membrane. The resulting concentration therefore depends on how well those fields represent the full collection area. The protocol tested recovery with standard particles, which supports the collection workflow, but the stated filter pore size alone is not proof of complete and equal detection at that size for every shape or polymer.{{cite:s-65f1d8743aef}}

The reviewed artifact is a repository author manuscript with line numbers and figure descriptions. Its representative-results section gives the range used here. It belongs to the same research program as earlier polypropylene bottle work and should not be counted as an independent replication of that earlier dataset. The available manuscript does not provide a numerical routine full-procedure blank distribution for every bottle test.{{cite:s-65f1d8743aef}}

Why total microparticles are not all microplastics

The cap experiment first collected material generated by repeated opening and closing, rinsing caps and necks with filtered ethanol. The extract was dried and diluted to a specified final volume before analysis. Laser direct infrared chemical imaging separated identified plastic polymers from cellulose, additives, and other particles. The paper’s total microparticle column is larger than its confirmed-plastic column and must not be quoted as if the two were equivalent.{{cite:s-80f7cd5b1cac}}

Smaller particles were imaged separately by electron microscopy. An image of a small object does not by itself establish that it is plastic, and those observations cannot extend the chemically confirmed infrared count into the nanoscale range. A size-bin statement in the discussion conflicts with the reported instrument window, so this page retains the clearly described infrared range instead.{{cite:s-80f7cd5b1cac}}

Why the studies cannot supply one bottle count

The experiments differ in handling, solvent, recovery, final volume, and chemical-identification method. One evaluates a hot-water preparation protocol; the other isolates abrasion from closures and necks. Neither result is a category-wide release rate. A high result for a tested specimen does not show that every product made of the same polymer behaves that way, and a low result in a larger-particle window does not establish absence of smaller material.{{cite:s-65f1d8743aef}}{{cite:s-80f7cd5b1cac}}

Both studies address particle generation. Neither follows exposed infants, measures uptake from the prepared liquid, or establishes a relationship between a bottle count and disease. Statements about material release should remain separate from decisions about feeding hygiene. These experiments do not test the health consequences of changing sterilization or formula-preparation procedures.{{cite:s-65f1d8743aef}}{{cite:s-80f7cd5b1cac}}

Regulatory status

The supplied EU restriction addresses defined synthetic polymer microparticles as substances or intentionally present in mixtures, with exclusions, derogations and transition provisions. A shedding measurement from an article does not by itself establish whether that restriction applies or has been violated.{{cite:s-2f1daf6ca78b}} The drinking-water methods are useful analytical comparisons, but they are not validated product-specific release tests for this category.{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}} No universal compliant particle count is inferred from them. Read the regulatory source guide.

What remains uncertain

The reviewed evidence does not provide a representative exposure distribution across all feeding bottles, a reliable count for every particle size, or a clinical threshold for these mixtures. More comparable tests using intact products and realistic food matrices would improve generalization. For now, the clearest interpretation keeps each result attached to its actual protocol and reports the missing information directly.{{cite:s-65f1d8743aef}}{{cite:s-80f7cd5b1cac}}

title: Microplastics in tea bags
scope: Plastic filter bags, strings, and particle dynamics during water contact
description: What Raman imaging and particle-dynamics experiments establish about tea-bag materials, release, and method-dependent findings.
body:
Laboratory studies have identified synthetic polymer particles in water exposed to some tea-filter bags. Other experiments follow suspended material from cut pieces of bag fabric over longer soaking and aging periods. The methods do not count the same size range or chemically confirm the same fraction of particles. Their findings cannot be combined into a single number for a cup of tea.{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}{{cite:s-bf013e1859f6}}

What this page covers

This page focuses on bag material and strings rather than treating all tea contamination as bag release. The strongest directly reviewed sources include Raman imaging of filter-bag soaking water and a study of particle behavior after bag materials contact water. One identifies polymer chemistry in imaged regions; the other follows changes in particle size and concentration in suspension. They answer related but different questions.{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}{{cite:s-bf013e1859f6}}

The term tea bag also covers different constructions. A woven nylon mesh, a nonwoven polypropylene filter, and cellulose paper do not share one composition or physical structure. Strings can have another composition. Bulk material identification is therefore a starting point, while chemical analysis of detached particles provides more direct evidence about what was released.{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}{{cite:s-bf013e1859f6}}

What the studies found

Raman imaging detected PET, polypropylene, nylon, and polyethylene in soaking samples from selected filter bags. Its multichannel fitting method resolved signals that a simpler single-peak map missed. Detection depended on the imaging and analysis workflow, rather than on a visible-particle count alone.{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and measurement limits.

Study and endpointReported findingMethod and contextLimit
Filter-bag soaking and chemical imaging{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}{{claim:s-344cfd824c7e-positive-soaks}}Raman spectra with multichannel fitting in selected regionsDetection frequency under study conditions; not a market-wide percentage or particles per cup.
Bag-material particle dynamics{{cite:s-bf013e1859f6}}Suspended-particle behavior differed among nylon, PP, and cellulose materialsBulk IR/thermal identification plus DLS and nanoparticle trackingCut bag squares and prolonged aging; not individual chemical confirmation of every suspended particle.

How the Raman study identified polymers

The investigators examined selected nonwoven PET and PP bags and woven nylon bags, including their strings. In the release experiment, individual bags were soaked in ultrapure water across specified temperatures and durations. The liquid was filtered, and Raman imaging examined selected regions where material had collected. Reference spectra helped distinguish overlapping polymer signals.{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}

This study also used a separate mixed-material preparation to optimize imaging. Counts from that optimization describe the particles identified in selected image regions. They are not a whole-bag release result or a measured count per serving. Treating a method-comparison count as a consumer dose would change both its denominator and its purpose.{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}

Observed particle composition did not always match the main bag polymer alone. The study linked some material to strings and particles already attached to surfaces. It did not establish that each detached particle had newly formed by heat degradation. The reported lack of a clear association with soaking conditions applies to this product set and analysis, and should not become a claim that temperature never affects release.{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}

What the particle-dynamics study adds

The later study first established bulk bag composition using infrared and thermal methods. It then cut cleaned bag material into squares and followed suspended particles during soaking and subsequent storage. Dynamic light scattering measured hydrodynamic behavior, while nanoparticle tracking provided concentration information for selected material types. Cellulose and synthetic-polymer systems behaved differently over time.{{cite:s-bf013e1859f6}}

These measurements extend the discussion beyond particles selected on microscope filters, but they carry different limitations. Bulk identification of nylon or polypropylene in a bag does not demonstrate the chemistry of every object scattering light in its soaking water. A light-scattering size is also not the same measurement as the longest dimension in a dried microscopy image. The source’s precise nanoparticle-tracking table is in supporting information not reviewed here, so this page does not reproduce an exact nanoscale count from it.{{cite:s-bf013e1859f6}}

Some experiments involved extended heating or aging after the bag material had been removed. Those conditions help study particle evolution, aggregation, or disappearance from the measured suspension. They do not reproduce the timing of every ordinary cup. A reduced signal from a cellulose sample should not be generalized to all materials or interpreted as measured elimination from a human body.{{cite:s-bf013e1859f6}}

Why published numbers differ

Counts depend on whether investigators use intact or opened bags, rinse before exposure, retain the strings, image an entire filter or selected areas, and require particle-specific chemistry. Counting smaller objects can change an abundance without showing that the tested bag released more material by mass. Conversely, polymer mass does not supply a particle count unless a study makes and states a model connecting them.{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}{{cite:s-bf013e1859f6}}

Cellulose-derived particles remain separate from synthetic plastic in this synthesis. Finding small material from a paper-based bag is not sufficient to call all of it microplastic. Likewise, a polymer label does not establish that a bag releases nothing: the relevant finding must come from the actual water-contact experiment and the method’s observation window.{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}{{cite:s-bf013e1859f6}}

Regulatory status

The supplied EU restriction addresses defined synthetic polymer microparticles as substances or intentionally present in mixtures, with exclusions, derogations and transition provisions. A shedding measurement from an article does not by itself establish whether that restriction applies or has been violated.{{cite:s-2f1daf6ca78b}} The drinking-water methods are useful analytical comparisons, but they are not validated product-specific release tests for this category.{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}} No universal compliant particle count is inferred from them. Read the regulatory source guide.

What remains uncertain

The selected studies do not establish one release rate across tea-bag constructions, a complete count across the microplastic and nanoplastic ranges, or a human health effect from drinking the tested infusions. Neither a cell experiment nor a water-release result provides a clinical threshold for consumers. The useful conclusion is narrower: synthetic polymers can be detected in some bag-contact samples, and measurement design strongly affects what is observed.{{cite:s-344cfd824c7e}}{{cite:s-bf013e1859f6}}

title: Microplastics in bottled water
scope: Retail-water occurrence and bottling-process sources
description: Raman and FTIR findings in bottled water, with source-specific particle counts, size windows, blank controls, and uncertainty.
body:
Studies have chemically identified plastic particles in bottled water, including water sold in glass bottles. The particles can arise from closures or processing as well as the bottle body. Counts vary with the sampled products, particle-size window, and analytical method. The reviewed findings establish occurrence and possible entry points, without supplying a universal concentration or a measured human health effect.{{cite:s-6f1a18e62816}}{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}

What this page covers

This page compares two complementary designs. A process-tracing study sampled mineral-water production from groundwater to the finished bottle. A retail survey analyzed water sold in PET, recycled PET, and returnable glass. The first can investigate where particles enter a particular production system. The second describes what was found in selected finished products. Their different sampling designs prevent a direct material ranking across studies.{{cite:s-6f1a18e62816}}{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}

The term bottled water describes the beverage and its full packaging system. A glass body can still use plastic sealing material. Finding polyethylene in glass-packaged water therefore does not mean the analyst identified glass as plastic. It raises a source question about closures or other contact materials, which must be investigated separately.{{cite:s-6f1a18e62816}}{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}

What the studies found

Scroll horizontally for methods and measurement limits.

Study and sampleReported particlesIdentification and size contextInterpretation
Process tracing: filled/capped reusable glass bottles{{cite:s-6f1a18e62816}}{{claim:s-6f1a18e62816-capped-mineral-water}}FPA-FTIR imaging; particles ≥11 µmSource-specific result at studied bottling facilities, with blank-based thresholds.
Retail survey: single-use PET-packaged water{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}{{claim:s-e8627d56229c-pet-water-mean}}Raman confirmation of detected particles; predominant sizes 20-100 µmMean ± SD of pooled analytical samples after polymer-specific control subtraction.
Retail survey: returnable-glass-packaged water{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}{{claim:s-e8627d56229c-glass-water-mean}}Same retail-study Raman workflowPlastic can enter glass packaging; no universal glass-versus-PET ranking follows.

Tracing entry during bottling

The process study collected raw and treated water, bottle-washing solutions, cleaned bottles, and finished filled/capped bottles. It also sampled filled bottles before capping at one facility. A marked increase after closure application, together with chemical resemblance to polyethylene seal material, supported closure abrasion as an important source in the sampled systems.{{cite:s-6f1a18e62816}}

The workflow used infrared imaging, automated spectral classification, and manual review. It tested size detection and particle recovery rather than assuming that filter pore size alone defined the observed range. Procedural blanks were present, and separate detection thresholds were calculated for different sample types. A value below such a threshold means the method could not distinguish a count confidently from its background. It does not establish that every particle was absent.{{cite:s-6f1a18e62816}}

The study also identified nonplastic material and discussed contamination associated with the sampling apparatus. This distinction is important because a particle seen on a filter can be cellulose, mineral material, or another substance. Only the chemically assigned plastic group belongs in the microplastic concentration used here.{{cite:s-6f1a18e62816}}

What the retail survey measured

The retail survey pooled bottle contents by product and market into analytical samples. Analysts located particles across the filter and used Raman spectra to assess each detected particle’s identity. They subtracted control findings according to the polymer identified, rather than counting every observed object as plastic. Fragments predominated, and the most common observed size classes were above the smallest particles detectable by Raman in principle.{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}

PET appeared prominently in PET-packaged samples. Polyethylene, including material with additive-related signals, was prominent in the recycled-PET and glass groups, consistent with possible closure contributions. That chemistry can suggest a source but does not by itself isolate where a particle entered the water. The retail design did not follow every bottling stage as the process study did.{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}

Pooling also changes interpretation. An analytical mean over pooled samples is not a guarantee for a particular bottle purchased later. Variability can reflect product, packaging, processing, or market differences. The paper’s recycled-PET mean differs slightly between the abstract and results text, so this page does not repeat a precise recycled-PET concentration until that discrepancy is resolved.{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}

Why the concentrations differ

The process and retail studies sampled different systems and used different identification workflows. Their size coverage, recovery, filter handling, spectral classification, and blank correction also differ. A lower concentration in one study cannot demonstrate that its packaging material inherently sheds less across all uses. It may reflect real product differences, analytical differences, or both.{{cite:s-6f1a18e62816}}{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}

Neither study provides a complete nanoplastic count. An instrument’s ability to identify a small reference particle is not equivalent to complete capture, detection, and chemical assignment of every environmental particle at that size. Counts per liter must stay attached to the stated observation window and should not be combined with smaller-particle estimates from another technique as though they formed a single validated measurement.{{cite:s-6f1a18e62816}}{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}

Regulatory status

The EU decision adopts a measurement methodology for water intended for human consumption, while California’s supplied methods describe analysis in treated drinking water. Their scope, size coverage and quality-control requirements matter when comparing these papers.{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}}{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}} The supplied California handbook copy is dated before its adoption meeting; its proposed monitoring calendar is not presented as the verified current timetable.{{cite:s-f4ab6cdc2d0b}} These documents are not used here as a health-based particle ceiling or as proof that a particular bottled-water product falls within a public-water monitoring program. Read the scope notes.

What remains uncertain

These studies do not establish an internal human dose, a clinical effect, or a safe or unsafe count for bottled water. Their most direct contribution is evidence of occurrence and, in the process study, a supported entry mechanism in selected facilities. Broader representative sampling and compatible validated methods are needed to determine how well a given concentration describes other products, locations, and particle sizes.{{cite:s-6f1a18e62816}}{{cite:s-e8627d56229c}}

title: Microplastics in salt
scope: Commercial edible salts and particle-identification limits
description: What Raman and infrared studies found in edible salts, including size thresholds, nonplastic particles, and differing material classifications.
body:
Chemical analyses have identified plastic particles in selected commercial salts. Sea salt is not the only salt type in the literature: retail studies also include rock, black, table, and pink salts. Reported counts depend strongly on the extraction size threshold, particle selection, and definition of plastic. These findings do not supply a universal salt concentration or establish a health effect from consuming the tested products.{{cite:s-d5adaa4c2600}}{{cite:s-4232fea69f85}}

What this page covers

This page uses direct studies of edible commercial salts. Research on salt-marsh sediment, hypersaline ecosystems, or salt solutions used to extract particles from soil does not measure a retail salt ingredient and is not substituted for food results. A salt’s source environment can inform hypotheses about contamination, but product occurrence still requires examination of the salt itself.

The selected studies differ in how finely they could extract and identify material. One intentionally used a coarse filter because finer filters clogged with salt-associated insoluble material. Another investigated smaller particles with microscopy and infrared spectroscopy. These are different observation windows, not competing measurements of the same salt sample.{{cite:s-d5adaa4c2600}}{{cite:s-4232fea69f85}}

What the studies found

Scroll horizontally for methods and measurement limits.

Study and endpointReported resultSize and chemistryLimit
Multi-country retail-salt study{{cite:s-d5adaa4c2600}}{{claim:s-d5adaa4c2600-confirmed-selection}}Coarse extraction above 149 µm; micro-Raman of selected particlesPigments, amorphous carbon, and unidentified spectra were not all counted as confirmed plastic.
Selected salt types sold in Australia{{cite:s-4232fea69f85}}{{claim:s-4232fea69f85-salt-average}}Observed particles 23.2 µm-3.9 mm; microscopy and selected ATR-FTIRAuthor MP category includes rayon/cellulose acetate; not a strict synthetic-only population estimate.

Why chemical identification changes the result

In the multi-country study, researchers dissolved salt, filtered insoluble particles, used a dense solution to separate material, and visually selected likely particles. Micro-Raman then tested the chemical composition of every selected object. Some objects were polypropylene or polyethylene, while others were pigments, carbon, or unresolved material. The confirmed-plastic subset was therefore smaller than the visually suspected subset.{{cite:s-d5adaa4c2600}}

A lake-salt sample could not be analyzed because insoluble material blocked the filter. Excluding that sample is different from recording a nondetect. Likewise, failure to identify a spectrum does not prove that the object was plastic or that it was harmless. The paper reports those categories separately, and this page retains that distinction.{{cite:s-d5adaa4c2600}}

The original paper also required a published correction because the plastic-polymer and pigment panels in a figure were inverted. The correction is a companion to the same dataset, not a new sampling study. This page uses the original results text for the numerical finding and records the correction so that readers do not confuse the figure panels.{{cite:s-d5adaa4c2600}}{{cite:s-1255af89193a}}

Evidence beyond sea salt

The Australia-market study sampled several terrestrial and marine salt types. It dissolved salt, used peroxide treatment, filtered the samples, and examined retained material by microscopy and fluorescence staining. Selected particles were then analyzed by ATR-FTIR. The measured average belongs to that selected set and is not a representative estimate for every salt sold nationally.{{cite:s-4232fea69f85}}

The authors identified synthetic polymers including polyamide and polyurethane. Their classification also included rayon and cellulose acetate. Because natural and regenerated cellulose are not interchangeable with persistent synthetic plastics, this page labels the numerical result as study-classified particles and explains the material definition. The same category label in two papers need not represent identical particle chemistry.{{cite:s-4232fea69f85}}

Some small particles did not yield usable infrared spectra, and the researchers excluded material below their effective spectroscopic size limit from quantification. The filter’s small pore size therefore should not be described as the validated particle-identification cutoff. SEM with elemental analysis supplied additional morphology and elemental information, but carbon and oxygen signals alone cannot distinguish a plastic fiber from natural material.{{cite:s-4232fea69f85}}

Blank controls and measurement quality

The multi-country study used covered equipment, cleaned materials, filtered reagents, and procedural controls for water and density-separation solution. The Australia-market study processed procedural blanks alongside the salts and reported no particles in those controls. These precautions reduce laboratory contamination, but they do not eliminate other limitations such as visual selection, incomplete recovery, or ambiguous spectra.{{cite:s-d5adaa4c2600}}{{cite:s-4232fea69f85}}

The second study pooled particles within salt type for spectroscopic selection. Its counts and chemical assignments should be read with that sampling procedure in mind. An average and standard deviation describe variability in the studied set; they do not define a maximum for future purchases or a concentration in an individual serving. No new serving-dose calculation is made here.{{cite:s-4232fea69f85}}

Why salt studies should remain separate

A coarse-filter count cannot establish the absence of smaller particles. A broader small-particle count may also use another material definition or chemistry-selection rule. Combining these results into a category average would hide those differences. Neither study establishes whether a particular particle entered during salt formation, processing, handling, or packaging solely from its presence in a finished product.{{cite:s-d5adaa4c2600}}{{cite:s-4232fea69f85}}

Regulatory status

The supplied EFSA statement is a dated scientific assessment that calls for improved methods and quality assurance. Its historical legislative description is not treated as a complete statement of current law. Neither that assessment nor the drinking-water measurement decision supplies a particle limit for this food category.{{cite:s-aa0dd4c46340}}{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}} A research concentration is not a product compliance determination. See source scope and versions.

What remains uncertain

The selected evidence does not establish a reliable contamination ranking for every salt source, complete coverage of nanoscale material, or a clinical outcome from salt-associated particles. The older paper’s health reassurance is not adopted as a measured finding because it did not test human outcomes. The defensible conclusion is that confirmed polymers occur in some tested salts and that precise counts require explicit size, material, and analytical context.{{cite:s-d5adaa4c2600}}{{cite:s-4232fea69f85}}

title: Microplastics in beer
scope: Beer measurements and related beverage-method context
description: What a beer survey measured, how estimates depend on polymer subsampling, and why other beverage studies cannot supply a universal beer count.
body:
An exploratory study that included Ecuadorian beer identified synthetic polymers in a pooled food-category subsample and reported estimated particle concentrations for craft and industrial beer. Those estimates are based on subsampling and extrapolation. They are not counts in which every observed object was confirmed as plastic. The reviewed evidence does not establish a typical concentration for beer sold elsewhere or a human health effect from drinking the tested beers.{{cite:s-b7ebe8a29311}}

What this page covers

Beer is a finished beverage with ingredients, brewing equipment, filtration, and packaging that may all affect particle observations. A food or beverage paper belongs on this page only when its actual samples include beer or when it provides clearly labeled methodological context. Milk, soda, cold tea, and experiments on empty beverage cups do not become beer measurements because they were filed in the same library folder.

What the beer study found

Diaz-Basantes and colleagues examined beer alongside honey, skim milk, and soft drinks. The beer samples were packaged in glass, and the authors separated craft and industrial processing groups. The paper reports the following category averages. Both carry the same limitation: the plastic share came from chemical analysis of a selected fraction of the observed objects, rather than confirmation of each counted object.{{cite:s-b7ebe8a29311}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limitations.

Sample groupPaper-reported estimateMeasurement basisInterpretation
Craft beer{{claim:s-b7ebe8a29311-craft-beer-estimate}}Microscopy with FTIR subsamplingExploratory source estimate; no universal craft-beer rate.
Industrial beer{{claim:s-b7ebe8a29311-industrial-beer-estimate}}Microscopy with FTIR subsamplingDifferent processing group, with no basis for a current market ranking.

Across the food categories, FTIR identified plastic in {{claim:s-b7ebe8a29311-confirmed-subsample}}. The remaining analyzed material included cellulose and inorganic objects. The source extrapolated this plastic fraction to the wider microscopic observations. That distinction matters: a table of fibers and fragments records particle appearance, while the polymer estimate depends on a separate identification step. The denominator in the chemical subsample is not a count of beer samples.{{cite:s-b7ebe8a29311}}

How the particles were measured

The workflow diluted the beverage, used sieving and hydrogen peroxide treatment, filtered the sample, and used sonication during particle transfer. Optical microscopy counted objects and recorded dimensions. FTIR then provided a chemical fingerprint for a selected set. The paper identified polypropylene, low- and high-density polyethylene, and polyacrylamide across the analyzed foods. It does not show that every polymer occurred at the same proportion in each beer.{{cite:s-b7ebe8a29311}}

The dimensions attached to the raw fiber and fragment observations should not be presented as a chemically confirmed beer-plastic size distribution. Sample preparation also involves sieving, filters, heating, and transfers. A filter pore size alone cannot establish complete recovery or a validated minimum size for identified plastics. This page therefore does not assign a precise polymer-confirmed size window to the beer estimates.{{cite:s-b7ebe8a29311}}

Contamination and comparison limits

The researchers described air cleaning, laminar flow, and blank runs. Fibers were found in the procedural blanks, and the inspected methods do not clearly show how those counts were subtracted from the beverage estimates. The article also differs between its methods sample count and the beer rows in its results table. Those limitations narrow how confidently the reported averages can be used.{{cite:s-b7ebe8a29311}}

A separate South African beverage study adds context on identification. It used microscopy, exclusion staining for natural material, and Raman analysis of a selected fraction. It found several synthetic polymers across alcoholic and nonalcoholic samples and could not assign contamination to one packaging material. Its main methods group the alcoholic samples together, so that aggregate is not used here as a beer-specific concentration. This keeps a category label from becoming a stronger claim than the source supports.{{cite:s-cb575acb0f42}}

What the findings do and do not establish

Glass packaging does not itself demonstrate that the liquid contains no plastic particles. Equally, detection in glass-packaged beer does not identify the cap, brewery equipment, source water, or airborne fallout as the proven cause. Distinguishing these routes would require comparisons designed to isolate them. The beer survey measured material in products; it did not measure absorption, disease, or a clinical response in drinkers.{{cite:s-b7ebe8a29311}}{{cite:s-cb575acb0f42}}

The available review supports an evidence page, with the estimates visibly qualified, rather than a single score for all beer. More direct beer studies with comprehensive polymer confirmation, numerical blank reporting, validated size coverage, and well-described sampling are needed to test whether results agree across products and places. The current numbers should remain attached to their source, method, and processing group.

Regulatory status

The supplied EFSA statement is a dated scientific assessment that calls for improved methods and quality assurance. Its historical legislative description is not treated as a complete statement of current law. Neither that assessment nor the drinking-water measurement decision supplies a particle limit for this food category.{{cite:s-aa0dd4c46340}}{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}} A research concentration is not a product compliance determination. See source scope and versions.

title: Microplastics in honey
scope: Honey surveys and plastic-pouch storage experiments
description: Source-specific honey counts, limited polymer confirmation, packaging evidence, and uncertainty without a pooled concentration.
body:
Studies have reported plastic particles in honey, but their measurements answer different questions. A Malaysian survey supplied microscopy-based counts with limited FTIR confirmation. A separate pouch-storage experiment identified particles with spectra matching packaging. These studies do not establish one concentration for honey, and neither measured human health outcomes.{{cite:s-e90dfcc63831}}{{cite:s-6776e996b5cf}}

What this page covers

Honey is both a biological product and a food that is harvested, processed, and packaged. An occurrence survey measures what was recovered from selected honey samples. A storage experiment asks whether the material found after specified storage is consistent with the package. These designs should remain distinct. Studies of sugar, bee behavior, or soil are not substituted for measurements of honey.

What the survey found

Ibrahim and colleagues compared honey from stingless bees and honey bees in Malaysia. Samples came from farms and stores. The paper reports the following means for objects classified as microplastics under microscopy. The means include visually counted fibers and fragments; they are not totals in which each object received chemical identification.{{cite:s-e90dfcc63831}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limitations.

Honey groupReported countMethodImportant qualification
Stingless-bee honey{{claim:s-e90dfcc63831-stingless-count}}Digestion, filtration, stereomicroscopyPE confirmed only in a selected particle subsample.
Honey-bee honey{{claim:s-e90dfcc63831-honeybee-count}}Same workflowGroup differences cannot isolate bee species from environment, processing, or packaging.

Fibers were the predominant observed form. The results discuss size classes spanning small fibers through millimeter-scale objects, while the abstract provides a narrower summary range. One result-specific size estimate for stingless-bee honey was {{claim:s-e90dfcc63831-stingless-size}}. It should be read as a dimension of the microscopy-classified material, with the paper’s identification limits retained, rather than a size distribution for fully confirmed plastic.{{cite:s-e90dfcc63831}}

How much chemical confirmation was done

The survey diluted honey, used hydrogen peroxide digestion, and filtered the resulting material before microscope examination. Selected objects underwent a hot-needle test, surface imaging, and FTIR analysis. The authors state that only {{claim:s-e90dfcc63831-ftir-selected}} could be chemically identified because of size limitations, and those objects were polyethylene. This establishes polyethylene presence in the selected material. It does not demonstrate that every counted fiber was polyethylene or that naturally derived fibers were absent.{{cite:s-e90dfcc63831}}

The reported contamination precautions included covered equipment, filtered solutions, rinsing, an airborne-control filter, and a room with air filtration. The inspected methods and results do not provide numerical blank counts, a correction calculation, or recovery validation sufficient to turn the visual total into an individually confirmed polymer count. This is a material limitation when fibers dominate a sample.{{cite:s-e90dfcc63831}}

What the pouch experiment adds

Katsara and colleagues studied honey in flexible plastic pouches under outdoor, refrigerator, and dark/dry storage conditions. Their workflow used dilution, controlled warming, peroxide, density separation, and successive filters. Raman spectra of recovered particles were compared with the packaging. The inner material was polyethylene, with polyethylene terephthalate associated with the outer packaging. This offers product-specific evidence consistent with packaging-related contamination.{{cite:s-6776e996b5cf}}

The paper also reports numerical particle estimates, but no pouch-release count is accepted on this page. The analysis used selected regions of filters with different particle densities and extrapolated beyond those fields. Some runs were marked as contaminated by a reagent container. Honey crystallization and sample recovery changed with storage, and results differed between batches. These details prevent a simple statement that storage always produces the same rate of increase.{{cite:s-6776e996b5cf}}

The study separately used GC-MS to identify extractable chemicals. A dissolved chemical result is not a microplastic count, and it is not interchangeable with the Raman particle evidence. The inspected article does not justify turning those chemical findings into a particle mass exposure for consumers.{{cite:s-6776e996b5cf}}

How to interpret the evidence

The survey counts are normalized to honey mass. Older exploratory honey results used a liquid-volume denominator and broad FTIR extrapolation across several foods. Those values cannot be compared directly or converted with an assumed honey density. Differences in digestion, object selection, size coverage, and chemical identification can explain part of the variation before any conclusion is made about geography or product quality.{{cite:s-e90dfcc63831}}{{cite:s-b7ebe8a29311}}

A useful next step is independent confirmation using representative honey sampling, quantified blanks, recovery tests, consistent dimensions, and chemical identification that covers the counted material. Until then, the evidence supports carefully labeled source results and packaging experiments. It does not support a typical serving count, a category-wide health claim, or an assurance based only on the absence of a visible particle.{{cite:s-e90dfcc63831}}{{cite:s-6776e996b5cf}}

Regulatory status

The supplied EFSA statement is a dated scientific assessment that calls for improved methods and quality assurance. Its historical legislative description is not treated as a complete statement of current law. Neither that assessment nor the drinking-water measurement decision supplies a particle limit for this food category.{{cite:s-aa0dd4c46340}}{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}} A research concentration is not a product compliance determination. See source scope and versions.

title: Microplastics in tap water
scope: Public drinking-water and distribution-system measurements
description: Blank-corrected counts, polymer identification, particle-size limits, and natural-fiber distinctions in selected drinking-water studies.
body:
Chemically identified microplastics have been reported in drinking-water distribution systems. The amount that can be distinguished from laboratory contamination depends on the sampling and identification method. Reviewed studies from Sweden and Denmark illustrate both findings and limits: a blank-corrected distribution-system measurement and a study in which larger particle observations could not be separated from background contamination.{{cite:s-41d8667b76f0}}{{cite:s-ebd2006452ff}}

What this page covers

Tap water means drinking water sampled from a public supply or a connected distribution point. It is not the same sample as river water, wastewater, bottled water, or water deliberately spiked with plastic for a detection-method experiment. The studies below were selected for their explicit chemical identification and quality-control reporting. This is a selected literature synthesis, not an exhaustive survey of every public water supply.

What the studies found

Kirstein and colleagues followed a Swedish waterworks and connected distribution pipes. They analyzed particle counts by infrared imaging and polymer mass by a separate thermal method. Their count result was corrected with station-specific blanks. Feld and colleagues used a closed tap-sampling system in Denmark, screened larger objects visually, and checked selected objects chemically.{{cite:s-41d8667b76f0}}{{cite:s-ebd2006452ff}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limitations.

Study and endpointReported resultSize contextInterpretation
Swedish distribution-system count{{claim:s-41d8667b76f0-system-count}}{{claim:s-41d8667b76f0-observed-major-size}}Blank-corrected system average, with variable station results.
Danish larger-object identity check{{claim:s-ebd2006452ff-large-confirmation}}Larger visually selected objectsMost examined objects were cellulosic; this is not a plastic concentration.
Danish selected small-particle analysis{{claim:s-ebd2006452ff-small-observed}}{{claim:s-ebd2006452ff-small-size}}Observed in analyzed filter portions; PET and rubber also occurred in blanks.

The Swedish method used {{claim:s-41d8667b76f0-nominal-floor}} for identification under its image-processing rule. Its observed size range was evaluated using uncorrected detections, while its concentration used blank subtraction. Those are different analytical datasets. The size distribution therefore must not be described as though background particles had been removed from every size class.{{cite:s-41d8667b76f0}}

Why the blanks matter

In the Swedish investigation, researchers measured contamination alongside sample groups and subtracted counts by polymer. Some corrected count values became zero. This does not establish that the original water contained absolutely no plastic; it means that the subtraction method did not leave a positive count under those conditions. The study also found differences between infrared-derived estimates and direct thermal polymer-mass measurements at low concentrations.{{cite:s-41d8667b76f0}}

The Danish study calculated a larger-object detection threshold of {{claim:s-ebd2006452ff-large-lod}}. All water samples stayed below that threshold for the visual endpoint. Chemical analysis showed that many objects that looked like plastic were cellulose. A result described as MP-like should therefore remain MP-like unless spectroscopy confirms polymer identity. A low visual total cannot simply be reported as a confirmed plastic concentration.{{cite:s-ebd2006452ff}}

The additional smaller-particle analysis examined selected filter areas from selected locations. Its identified fragments show that a larger-object screen does not describe all size classes. At the same time, the presence of polymer material in a blank means that the smaller analysis cannot be used as an uncomplicated measure of contamination-free water sampling. The paper calls for broader assessment and more complete filter analysis.{{cite:s-ebd2006452ff}}

What the methods measure

Infrared imaging matches a particle’s spectrum with reference material and supplies dimensions. Thermal analysis breaks down polymers and measures chemical signals associated with polymer mass. Particle count, modeled mass from a particle’s shape, and directly measured polymer mass answer different questions. They cannot be substituted for each other with an assumed particle density or a representative diameter.{{cite:s-41d8667b76f0}}

Sampling volume, filter transfer, the fraction of a filter scanned, reference-library coverage, and the minimum-pixel rule all affect what can be reported. Closed sampling reduces opportunities for contamination but does not remove the need for blanks. Natural fibers, rubber from equipment, and uncertain spectra also require explicit handling rather than being automatically included in a synthetic-plastic total.{{cite:s-ebd2006452ff}}{{cite:s-41d8667b76f0}}

What remains uncertain

These studies do not yield a universal tap-water count or a comparison of tap water with every bottled-water product. Their source waters, treatment systems, sample preparation, and size coverage differ. Neither study measures a human clinical outcome. Counts obtained in one system cannot determine the health effects of another supply, and a non-detection in a stated measurement window does not establish absence of smaller particles.{{cite:s-41d8667b76f0}}{{cite:s-ebd2006452ff}}

The most useful reading of a water result keeps the sampled location, volume basis, polymer-confirmation method, size coverage, and treatment of blanks together. More directly comparable monitoring can establish whether patterns persist across seasons and systems. Until that evidence is available, source-specific results should remain separate from claims about all drinking water.

Regulatory status

The EU decision adopts a measurement methodology for water intended for human consumption, while California’s supplied methods describe analysis in treated drinking water. Their scope, size coverage and quality-control requirements matter when comparing these papers.{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}}{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}} The supplied California handbook copy is dated before its adoption meeting; its proposed monitoring calendar is not presented as the verified current timetable.{{cite:s-f4ab6cdc2d0b}} These documents are not used here as a health-based particle ceiling or as proof that a particular bottled-water product falls within a public-water monitoring program. Read the scope notes.

title: Microplastics in infant food puree
scope: Finished infant puree: primary evidence gap
description: The supplied category contains a review only. No measured puree concentration is accepted; related foods and feeding products remain separate.
body:
The supplied infant-food-puree folder does not contain an original laboratory test of packaged puree. Its only paper is a review of microplastics and nanoplastics in infant diets and environments. This page therefore reports an evidence gap. It supplies no particle concentration, polymer distribution, size range, or product ranking for infant puree.{{cite:s-70a2257b7f9b}}

What this page covers

Infant puree means a prepared, blended food sold or served as puree, including food in a jar or pouch. Research on feeding bottles, water, powdered formula, raw produce, or breast milk addresses related questions, but it is not a direct measurement of finished puree. Those distinctions are especially important when a broad review uses the phrase baby food to discuss many ingredients and feeding routes.{{cite:s-70a2257b7f9b}}

What the supplied paper provides

Kadac-Czapska and colleagues summarize published work on infant exposure pathways, food-contact products, food ingredients, and biological effects. The review’s food tables include milk, formula, water, produce, meat, and flour, with measurements attributed to other papers. It does not describe its own collection of puree products, extraction from a puree matrix, numerical blanks, or polymer-confirmed puree particles.{{cite:s-70a2257b7f9b}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limitations.

Evidence in the folderWhat it can supportWhat is not established
Narrative review of infant dietsBackground questions and leads to original papersA measured concentration in finished infant puree.
Secondary tables covering other foodsIdentification of related matrices for source retrievalTransfer of ingredient counts to a jar, pouch, or serving.
Discussion of toxicology literatureRecognition that exposure and effect evidence differA clinical effect caused by consuming a tested puree.

Why no number is shown

A numerical result would need a primary experiment on the relevant product, a stated denominator, a measurement window, and chemical identification suited to the recovered particles. Extraction also needs to separate the food matrix from the particles without mistaking natural material for synthetic polymers. Counts from a raw ingredient cannot be added together to manufacture a puree result, and a bottle-release test cannot define what is already in the food.{{cite:s-70a2257b7f9b}}

What would close the gap

The next evidence needed is an original puree study with identifiable products or anonymized sample groups, particle recovery validation, numerical procedure blanks, clear size measurements, and polymer confirmation. Comparisons of packaging should test matched food under controlled conditions so that differences in ingredients or processing are not attributed to the container. No such primary dataset was available in this category folder.

This gap should not be read as proof that puree is particle-free or as evidence that it is unsafe. It means that the supplied material cannot support a quantitative product conclusion. The review itself emphasizes analytical and translation limits, including difficulty comparing methods and applying experimental toxicology to people. Related categories can be read separately while direct puree evidence is sought.{{cite:s-70a2257b7f9b}}

Regulatory status

The supplied EFSA statement is a dated scientific assessment that calls for improved methods and quality assurance. Its historical legislative description is not treated as a complete statement of current law. Neither that assessment nor the drinking-water measurement decision supplies a particle limit for this food category.{{cite:s-aa0dd4c46340}}{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}} A research concentration is not a product compliance determination. See source scope and versions.

title: Microplastics from cutting boards
scope: Plastic cutting boards and vendor-cut chicken and fish
description: A single-study assessment of polyethylene transfer into food, with source-specific counts, size context, and washing limitations.
body:
A market-based study found polyethylene material in chicken and fish cut on plastic boards, with color and polymer chemistry consistent with the boards used. It supports mechanical transfer as a plausible contamination route in those shops. It does not establish a typical release rate for every household cutting board or a health effect from the measured particles.{{cite:s-06b18fa11037}}

What this page covers

The supplied cutting-board folder contains a single original study. Its samples were food cut by vendors in markets and supermarkets in the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait. Researchers examined the food and corresponding board materials. These are observations of shop preparation, not a standardized experiment counting particles from each knife stroke or a survey of all kitchenware.{{cite:s-06b18fa11037}}

What the study found

Recovered fragments were measured by microscopy, and infrared analysis identified polyethylene in the extracted material. Board characterization also indicated polyethylene, with thermal and density information supporting a low-density assignment for the boards tested. Correspondence in color and composition supports the authors’ attribution to the cutting surface, while leaving the result specific to those samples and preparation practices.{{cite:s-06b18fa11037}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limitations.

Food sampleReported countCondition or sizeHow to read it
Chicken C2{{claim:s-06b18fa11037-chicken-c2}}{{claim:s-06b18fa11037-chicken-c2-size}}Table-specific triplicate result; not particles per cut.
King mackerel F6{{claim:s-06b18fa11037-fish-f6}}Before washingFood-normalized sample result.
King mackerel F6A{{claim:s-06b18fa11037-fish-f6-washed}}After the source washing procedureLower count in a limited comparison; remaining particles detected.

The chicken value shown is taken from the results table. The surrounding prose assigns the highest count to a different sample code, so this page uses the table label explicitly and does not combine the discrepancy into a category-wide maximum. The fish results also describe different species, cuts, and handling conditions. A count from one fish cannot stand in for every fish or a consumer serving.{{cite:s-06b18fa11037}}

How the food was analyzed

The investigators digested the meat with aqueous potassium hydroxide, filtered and washed the recovered material, and used microscopy to evaluate fragments. Image analysis supplied Feret dimensions, meaning the longest distance across a particle outline. Infrared analysis was performed on recovered material and board filings. The chemical comparison has more evidentiary value than color alone, since colored natural material can also appear in food.{{cite:s-06b18fa11037}}

The study describes cleaned equipment and surfaces, inspected filters, tested sample bags, protective clothing, and parallel blanks. Numerical blank results and a recovery-based adjustment were not provided in the inspected main methods. A filter pore size was reported, but that is not a validated lower detection limit for the entire workflow. Very small particles and any losses during digestion, transfer, and washing remain outside a complete account.{{cite:s-06b18fa11037}}

Washing and heating are separate questions

The king-mackerel comparison found a lower count after washing, with particles still present. That result cannot establish a reliable removal fraction across foods, cutting conditions, or kitchens. It also cannot show that rinsing makes a food free of microplastics. A handling comparison is distinct from a study measuring downstream health outcomes.{{cite:s-06b18fa11037}}

The authors also examined grilled fish and observed changes in particle form, including melting and fusion. A changed shape is not evidence that the polymer disappeared. However, the experiment does not provide a validated particle balance or a general conversion from raw-food counts to cooked-food exposure. Counts, fragment mass, and mechanical board-wear tests therefore remain separate endpoints.{{cite:s-06b18fa11037}}

How far the board attribution can go

In observed shop preparation, cutting through bone and cutting an existing fillet involve different forces. Boards also vary in wear and handling. The study’s evidence is consistent with fragments being introduced during cutting, but it does not isolate a single cause of variation across all samples. It cannot rank every board material, brand, or design, and its limited comparisons with other preparation surfaces do not constitute a broad product test.{{cite:s-06b18fa11037}}

The strongest supported conclusion is that the preparation surface can be a source of plastic material in food under the conditions examined. The number normalized to food mass should stay attached to the food sample and its method. Multiplying it by an assumed serving size, annual food consumption, or board lifetime would create a new estimate that this page does not make.

What remains uncertain

Independent studies with standardized cutting conditions, quantitative blank reporting, validated extraction recovery, and particle-by-particle polymer identification would improve comparability. Repeated-use board testing and matched food controls would help separate material, wear, cutting force, and transfer into food. Until then, this category retains a single-study scope. It documents measured fragments and their limitations without supplying a universal release number or an inference about disease.{{cite:s-06b18fa11037}}

Regulatory status

The supplied EU restriction addresses defined synthetic polymer microparticles as substances or intentionally present in mixtures, with exclusions, derogations and transition provisions. A shedding measurement from an article does not by itself establish whether that restriction applies or has been violated.{{cite:s-2f1daf6ca78b}} The drinking-water methods are useful analytical comparisons, but they are not validated product-specific release tests for this category.{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}} No universal compliant particle count is inferred from them. Read the regulatory source guide.

title: Microplastics in cosmetics and personal care
scope: Selected microbead-containing personal-care products
description: Source-specific particle measurements in selected scrubs, with polymer identification, method differences, and limits of label surveys.
body:
Selected personal-care products have contained plastic microbeads, and laboratory studies have measured particles recovered from those products. Their results depend on which products were selected and how particles were extracted, counted, and identified. The reviewed studies support product-specific findings. They do not establish that every cosmetic contains microplastics or that the measured particles penetrated human skin.{{cite:s-e13c6d651052}}{{cite:s-ee700e8b74e0}}

What this page covers

This page distinguishes deliberately selected microbead-containing personal-care products from a market-wide contamination estimate. A facial scrub with polyethylene listed in its ingredients is a different question from an unexpected plastic fragment in a cream. A label survey can identify products for further examination, but the printed name of a polymer is not a laboratory count or a measurement of particle dimensions.{{cite:s-e13c6d651052}}{{cite:s-ee700e8b74e0}}

What the studies measured

Renner and colleagues compared methods using selected toothpastes and facial scrubs labeled as containing polyethylene. Bashir and colleagues combined a historical ingredient-label survey in Macao with laboratory analysis of selected cleansers and scrubs. Bashir’s attempts to isolate and quantify particles from the cosmetic-product group were unsuccessful and were excluded from its laboratory results. The accepted measurements here concern the selected personal-care cleansers and scrubs. The table preserves each paper’s product code, measurement basis, and observed size range. It does not convert between the different product-mass denominators.{{cite:s-e13c6d651052}}{{cite:s-ee700e8b74e0}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limitations.

Sample and sourceReported countObserved dimensionsIdentification and caveat
Facial scrub FS2, methods comparison{{claim:s-e13c6d651052-facial-scrub-microscopy}}{{claim:s-e13c6d651052-facial-scrub-size}}µFTIR confirmed PE in selected fragments; light-microscopy count.
Facial scrub B, Macao study{{claim:s-ee700e8b74e0-scrub-b-table2}}{{claim:s-ee700e8b74e0-scrub-b-size}}LDPE assignment in Table 2; table and narrative differ.

The values from the Macao paper use its results table, which reports means and standard deviations. Nearby narrative gives slightly different point estimates and product descriptions. That discrepancy remains disclosed. These observations describe the tested historical products, not today’s formulation of any product and not a current prevalence figure for cosmetics in another market.{{cite:s-ee700e8b74e0}}

Why different instruments give different answers

The methods-comparison study separated particles from the product matrix and compared light microscopy, laser diffraction, and imaging flow cytometry. These approaches do not measure exactly the same feature. Microscopy measures visible outlines, diffraction characterizes scattering behavior, and flow cytometry detects events within the prepared suspension. Filter preselection and settling also changed the material that reached the instrument.{{cite:s-e13c6d651052}}

The resulting size distributions differed across methods. Flow-cytometry blanks had substantial background, and several products could not be quantified above that background with that approach. A blank-limited result is not a finding that the product contains no plastic. It also cannot be turned into a validated particle count by treating every detected event as a polymer. This page uses the paper’s microscopy result, with its own size context, rather than a mixture of instruments.{{cite:s-e13c6d651052}}

Infrared spectroscopy identified polyethylene in a selected fragment subsample. It did not chemically identify every object counted by microscopy. No microscopy blank particles were reported for that comparison, but the extraction was designed to compare counting approaches rather than to validate every polymer’s recovery from a broad range of formulas. These limitations remain relevant even when the selected products listed polyethylene.{{cite:s-e13c6d651052}}

Product findings and environmental findings differ

The Macao investigation separately examined coastal sediment and calculated potential emissions from product use. Sediment particles come from many sources and do not measure the quantity inside a cosmetic. Modeled emissions also depend on assumptions about use and wastewater treatment. Neither endpoint is substituted for the product table above. The described recovery and negative-control procedures for sediment should not be assumed to validate the product extraction without separate evidence.{{cite:s-ee700e8b74e0}}
