Microbeads selected from a product can have a different shape and size distribution from weathered environmental fragments. A list of polymer ingredients can also include materials with different physical forms. Meaningful comparisons need particle characterization, not simply a shared chemical name. The source methods and product selection explain why the reported results should stay attached to their tested matrices.{{cite:s-e13c6d651052}}{{cite:s-ee700e8b74e0}}

What remains uncertain

These product measurements did not assess skin absorption, blood concentrations, irritation, or a clinical outcome in users. A measured particle count cannot establish those effects. Studies of aquatic animals or environmental sediments are also not direct evidence of a human dermatological effect from the tested formulation. This page therefore reports material findings and method limitations without extending them to a health claim.{{cite:s-e13c6d651052}}{{cite:s-ee700e8b74e0}}

Broader product coverage, independently verified formulations, numerical product-workflow blanks, recovery validation, and well-defined analytical size windows would make future comparisons more informative. Until then, selected microbead products, incidental contamination, label surveys, and modeled environmental releases remain distinct evidence types. None supplies a single count for the whole cosmetics category.

Regulatory status

The supplied EU restriction concerns defined synthetic polymer microparticles, including applicable intentional uses in cosmetic mixtures. Product type, polymer definition, exemptions and transition provisions must be checked before drawing a legal conclusion.{{cite:s-2f1daf6ca78b}} A paper’s particle count or fiber-shedding experiment alone does not establish compliance. Water-testing procedures in the same folder do not set a particle limit for wipes or cosmetics.{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}} Read the scope and source-version notes.

title: Microplastics in fish and seafood
scope: Edible tissue, shellfish and processed fish
description: What edible-tissue studies found, with chemically identified particles, original denominators and limits.
body:
Studies have identified microplastics in some edible seafood tissues. What a consumer might eat depends on the tissue sampled, how the product was processed and the measurement method. A particle in a fish gut is a different finding from a particle in edible flesh. This page centers on studies that made that distinction, rather than treating every wildlife ingestion study as a food test.{{cite:s-d4417412ccc4}}{{cite:s-452a5f83f01d}}

What this page covers

The directly reviewed evidence includes commercial shellfish soft tissues and dried fish with flesh and organs analyzed separately. These results describe the tested specimens. They do not establish a common particle level for fish, shrimp, clams or mussels sold everywhere. Market location also needs care: a product bought in a country may have been harvested elsewhere. The shellfish study documented purchase locations, while noting uncertainty about some product origins.{{cite:s-d4417412ccc4}}

Edible tissue is especially important when interpreting seafood papers. Bivalve soft tissues may be consumed together, whereas fish gills and digestive organs may be removed. The dried-fish paper used “eviscerated flesh” to mean the fish remaining after removal of gills and viscera. That is broader than a sample of isolated muscle. Its finding cannot be relabeled as the concentration in a fresh fish fillet.{{cite:s-452a5f83f01d}}

What the studies found

The market shellfish survey reported {{claim:s-d4417412ccc4-prevalence}}. It analyzed edible tissues with microFTIR, a method that compares infrared spectra with reference polymers. The authors reported both a concentration across all tested individuals and a separate concentration for the subset containing particles. The table below uses the all-individual denominator. Excluding nondetections would answer a different question and make the average appear higher.{{cite:s-d4417412ccc4}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limits.

Study and materialReported resultMethod and size contextLimit
Commercial clams purchased in Korea{{cite:s-d4417412ccc4}}{{claim:s-d4417412ccc4-clam-korea}}Whole-filter microFTIR after digestion; {{claim:s-d4417412ccc4-analysis-size-limit}}Wet edible-tissue denominator; sampled lots only
Commercial mussels purchased in Belgium{{cite:s-d4417412ccc4}}{{claim:s-d4417412ccc4-mussel-belgium}}Same shellfish workflow; chemically matched particle spectraPurchase location is not necessarily harvest origin
Dried fish, separated fractions{{cite:s-452a5f83f01d}}{{claim:s-452a5f83f01d-confirmed}}; {{claim:s-452a5f83f01d-flesh}}; {{claim:s-452a5f83f01d-organs}}Micro-Raman on visual candidates; {{claim:s-452a5f83f01d-initial-sieve}}Totals across specimens and fractions, not particles per gram or per serving

The dried-fish study illustrates why a visual count should not automatically be called a plastic count. Its recovered candidates included confirmed polymers, pigments, nonplastic material and unidentified particles. Polypropylene and polyethylene were the most common confirmed plastic types, alongside polystyrene, polyethylene terephthalate and nylon. The study reported more plastic particles in the flesh fraction than the organ fraction for some species, but this finding applies to its dried products and preparation method.{{cite:s-452a5f83f01d}}

How the methods affect the answer

The shellfish investigators tested digestion efficiency and polymer recovery before applying their protocol. They used controlled preparation areas, air blanks and procedural blanks, and reported no confirmed plastic in the procedural blanks. They scanned the filter and chemically checked candidate particles. Those steps strengthen the distinction between polymer particles and residual biological material. They do not make the dataset representative of every seafood supply chain.{{cite:s-d4417412ccc4}}

The dried-fish investigators also used procedural blanks and reported no particles in them. Their process combined digestion, density separation and visual selection before Raman analysis. However, the initial sieve was coarser than the later collection filter. The later filter pore size cannot be treated as proof that all smaller particles in the original fish were recovered. Its total therefore cannot be compared directly with a study using a smaller validated analysis window.{{cite:s-452a5f83f01d}}

What the findings can establish

These studies support the presence of chemically identified particles in particular edible seafood samples. They do not identify the complete path a particle took into a product. Environmental uptake, postharvest handling, processing and packaging were not fully separated. Identifying a familiar polymer is insufficient to identify a specific product as its source.{{cite:s-d4417412ccc4}}{{cite:s-452a5f83f01d}}

Particle totals, particles per animal and particles per gram wet tissue retain different meanings. Cooking, serving size and digestion in the consumer were not measured in these comparisons. No dietary intake number is calculated here, and the occurrence results are not a demonstration that a particular meal caused illness. The strongest conclusion remains specific: the sampled edible tissues contained identifiable plastic particles within the capabilities of the methods used.{{cite:s-d4417412ccc4}}{{cite:s-452a5f83f01d}}

Regulatory status

The supplied EFSA statement is a dated scientific assessment that calls for improved methods and quality assurance. Its historical legislative description is not treated as a complete statement of current law. Neither that assessment nor the drinking-water measurement decision supplies a particle limit for this food category.{{cite:s-aa0dd4c46340}}{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}} A research concentration is not a product compliance determination. See source scope and versions.

title: Microplastics in environmental wildlife
scope: Local wildlife fecal monitoring
description: A narrow look at gull fecal monitoring, chemical confirmation and the limits of environmental indicators.
body:
The reviewed environmental-wildlife folder contains a local Armenian gull feces study. It reported visual particle candidates and confirmed polymer identity in selected larger particles. This is environmental monitoring evidence. It is not a test of food, household products, human samples or the health of individual birds.{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}

What was sampled

The study collected fecal deposits around the Lake Van Basin in Türkiye and selected {{claim:s-bc68ef9e4ee3-deposits}} for analysis. Deposits were combined into composite groups before processing. A fecal deposit is not equivalent to an independently identified bird. Repeated sampling from communal areas cannot establish the prevalence of particles in the local bird population without knowing which birds contributed the deposits.{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}

Fecal sampling can document material that animals excrete without requiring tissue removal. It does not measure the concentration retained in internal organs. The deposits may reflect ingested material and the setting in which the sample was collected, but the study did not track individual ingestion events or experimentally assign sources. A location associated with human activity is not itself proof of the origin of each particle.{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}

What the study found

The authors reported {{claim:s-bc68ef9e4ee3-suspects}} across the composite samples. The most frequent visual size category was the {{claim:s-bc68ef9e4ee3-largest-size-class}}. These are visual classifications. Chemical testing was performed on {{claim:s-bc68ef9e4ee3-ftirsample}}, using a larger-particle selection that did not cover the dominant small visual size class. The visual total should therefore be read as suspected particles with subset polymer support, rather than a chemically confirmed total.{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limits.

Study and materialReported resultMethod and size contextLimit
Armenian gull fecal composites{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}{{claim:s-bc68ef9e4ee3-suspects}}Digestion, filtration, stereomicroscopy and visual categorizationNo quantitative field or procedural blanks; composite observations
Selected larger fecal particle candidates{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}{{claim:s-bc68ef9e4ee3-ftirsample}}FTIR supported polymer identification in selected larger particlesSelection does not validate every particle in the visual count
Visual size distribution{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}{{claim:s-bc68ef9e4ee3-largest-size-class}}Image-based size classificationDominant class was below the stated chemical selection threshold

Chemical identity and contamination controls

The investigators used alkaline and oxidative digestion, followed by filtration and microscopic examination. FTIR identified polymers including polyethylene, polystyrene and polyethylene terephthalate among selected particles. Electron microscopy and elemental analysis examined surface appearance and composition. Surface erosion and a carbon-rich signal alone cannot uniquely establish that an object is a particular plastic polymer; FTIR supplies the more specific chemical evidence.{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}

The paper described cleaning equipment, using glass or metal tools, covering samples and wearing nonsynthetic laboratory clothing. It also explicitly stated that quantitative field and procedural controls were not performed. This leaves uncertainty about airborne fibers and other contamination introduced during collection or processing. Careful handling reduces opportunities for contamination, but it does not quantify the contamination that remained.{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}

What this environmental indicator means

The data can support a local observation that some particles recovered from gull feces were plastic polymers. Composite preparation limits individual-level interpretation, and partial chemical confirmation limits interpretation of the total count. The reported spatial differences should not become a ranking of individual bird exposure or a general estimate for wildlife elsewhere. The abstract and Methods also differ in how they describe the selected larger particles, so the exact selection should be checked before reuse in broader comparisons.{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}

No consumer exposure number follows directly from this result. Feces are not edible seafood tissue, and a wildlife indicator is not a human biomonitoring result. The study did not establish a human dose, a product-specific source or a clinical outcome. The page remains intentionally narrow because a single local source with these quality-control limits cannot support a general account of microplastics across all wildlife.{{cite:s-bc68ef9e4ee3}}

Regulatory status

The EU restriction addresses specified synthetic polymer microparticles in substances and mixtures. It does not set a wildlife-feces particle threshold or establish an ecological effect from an occurrence count.{{cite:s-2f1daf6ca78b}} Drinking-water technical methods require validation before extension to a different environmental or biological matrix.{{cite:s-b8033a33708a}} Read the source-scope guide.

title: Microplastics in household dust and air
scope: Settled household dust and suspended indoor particles
description: How indoor air and settled-dust studies measured particles, with size windows and contamination controls.
body:
Researchers have identified synthetic polymer particles in indoor air and settled household dust. Those are different sample types: air sampling measures particles suspended during collection, while floor-dust sampling describes accumulated material. Their results should not be combined into a single household particle count or assumed to represent a person's internal dose.{{cite:s-850d35272369}}{{cite:s-b77f33e84d3c}}

Air and dust answer different questions

The directly reviewed air study sampled French apartments and car cabins. Its Raman method targeted small suspended particles. The dust study examined {{claim:s-b77f33e84d3c-dustsamples}} from Japanese single-person residences, using sieving and microFTIR to identify selected objects. Dust that has settled on a floor includes a mixture of materials, including cellulose. A visible fiber can be natural material, a synthetic polymer or something the method cannot identify.{{cite:s-850d35272369}}{{cite:s-b77f33e84d3c}}

The sampling locations were selected study settings, not random samples of every residence or vehicle. Activities, ventilation, furnishings and the size range the instrument can analyze all affect which particles are recovered. Neither study establishes the origin of an individual particle simply because its polymer also occurs in household products. Source attribution requires additional evidence beyond matching a common polymer.{{cite:s-850d35272369}}{{cite:s-b77f33e84d3c}}

What the studies found

The indoor-air study reported {{claim:s-850d35272369-residential}} and {{claim:s-850d35272369-car}}. These are corrected and extrapolated concentrations rather than counts from the complete filter. Apartment particles had {{claim:s-850d35272369-apartment-size}}. Polyethylene was the leading identified apartment polymer; car samples had a different mixture that included polyamide, ABS, polyethylene and PET. The reported apartment-versus-car difference was not statistically significant, so these medians are not evidence that car cabins generally have a higher concentration.{{cite:s-850d35272369}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limits.

Study and materialReported resultMethod and size contextLimit
Apartment suspended air{{cite:s-850d35272369}}{{claim:s-850d35272369-residential}}Active sampling and Raman; {{claim:s-850d35272369-apartment-size}}Blank subtraction, recovery correction and filter-area extrapolation
Car-cabin suspended air{{cite:s-850d35272369}}{{claim:s-850d35272369-car}}Active sampling and Raman identificationSelected cabins; difference from apartments not statistically significant
Selected fibrous polymers in household floor dust{{cite:s-b77f33e84d3c}}{{claim:s-b77f33e84d3c-petshare}}Sieved dust fractions and microFTIR of selected particlesComposition of identified fibrous polymers, not percentage of total dust mass

The Japanese dust paper found a substantial cellulose component and several synthetic polymers. Among the identified fibrous polymers it reported {{claim:s-b77f33e84d3c-petshare}}; polyacrylonitrile and other synthetic materials were also present. This proportion does not mean the same fraction of all house dust was PET. The study analyzed selected particles within size fractions, so it cannot supply an unreported total particle concentration per gram or per room.{{cite:s-b77f33e84d3c}}

Why size and blank correction matter

The air investigators measured a small central area of each filter using Raman spectroscopy, then extrapolated to the effective filter area and divided by sampled air volume. They subtracted blank particles by polymer and size class and corrected for recovery loss. These controls address contamination and processing, while adding assumptions about particle distribution and recovery. Reference recovery beads were larger than many particles detected in real samples, which limits confidence that all size fractions behaved identically.{{cite:s-850d35272369}}

Small particles can be more numerous than larger fibers. An instrument that resolves smaller objects can therefore report a much larger concentration than a study targeting coarse fibers without showing a change in the underlying environment. This is why an air concentration should travel with its measured size window, sample conditions and analytical method. The paper's modeled nanoplastic concentrations and modeled inhalation totals are not treated here as directly observed measurements.{{cite:s-850d35272369}}

The settled-dust study used vacuum collection and selected particles from sieved fractions for microFTIR. It described clean laboratory handling, but a quantified procedural blank result was not located in the supplied main text. Some summary polymer percentages also differ across sections. This page uses the clearly defined fibrous-polymer result and avoids presenting a broad percentage for all household dust.{{cite:s-b77f33e84d3c}}

Presence is not a clinical result

These studies establish occurrence within their sampling and analysis limits. They did not measure how much material entered a person's circulation, identify every originating item or test whether a particular household caused disease. Floor-dust composition cannot be converted to an inhaled dose without measuring resuspension and breathing-zone air. The supported conclusion is that indoor particles include identifiable synthetic polymers, and that robust comparison requires matching the sample type, size window and method.{{cite:s-850d35272369}}{{cite:s-b77f33e84d3c}}

Regulatory status

The supplied EU restriction addresses defined synthetic polymer microparticles as substances or intentionally present in mixtures, with exclusions, derogations and transition provisions. A shedding measurement from an article does not by itself establish whether that restriction applies or has been violated.{{cite:s-2f1daf6ca78b}} The drinking-water methods are useful analytical comparisons, but they are not validated product-specific release tests for this category.{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}} No universal compliant particle count is inferred from them. Read the regulatory source guide.

title: Microplastics in human biomonitoring
scope: Human tissue detection and analytical uncertainty
description: What human tissue studies detected, how contamination was checked and what detection cannot establish.
body:
Human biomonitoring investigates whether material can be detected in biological samples. It does not test a consumer product, identify a specific source of exposure or establish that a detected particle caused disease. The reviewed studies illustrate both tissue-specific detection and the difficulty of ruling out contamination during clinical collection and laboratory processing.{{cite:s-d2f3af1338e5}}{{cite:s-d78cd56bfc44}}

What these studies measured

The evidence here includes a clinical pilot involving placenta and meconium and a postmortem case series involving the olfactory bulb. These tissues have different structures, sampling procedures and interpretation. A finding in one tissue cannot be converted into a whole-body burden or generalized to every person. The studies did not trace individual particles from a food package, bottle or garment into the tissue.{{cite:s-d2f3af1338e5}}{{cite:s-d78cd56bfc44}}

Biomonitoring results also depend on which polymer types the method can recognize and how the biological matrix is removed. A chemical spectrum needs to be distinguished from tissue constituents and from material introduced by sampling equipment. Where negative controls contain the same polymers as the specimens, simply subtracting an assumed background or reporting a positive label without the control information can conceal uncertainty.{{cite:s-d2f3af1338e5}}

What the studies found

The olfactory-bulb case series reported {{claim:s-d78cd56bfc44-occurrence}} and {{claim:s-d78cd56bfc44-total}}. Its nonfiber objects had {{claim:s-d78cd56bfc44-particle-size}}. Identified materials included polypropylene, polyamide or nylon, polyethylene and polyethylene vinyl acetate. A composite fiber was also reported. These findings were based on microFTIR examination of tissue sections and digested filters, with procedural and negative-control filters reported to contain no synthetic polymer particles.{{cite:s-d78cd56bfc44}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limits.

Study and materialReported resultMethod and size contextLimit
Postmortem olfactory bulb specimens{{cite:s-d78cd56bfc44}}{{claim:s-d78cd56bfc44-occurrence}}; {{claim:s-d78cd56bfc44-total}}MicroFTIR on cryosections and digested filters; {{claim:s-d78cd56bfc44-particle-size}}Small selected case series; no validated recovery test or nanoplastic measurement
Placenta and meconium clinical pilot{{cite:s-d2f3af1338e5}}Qualitative positive screening for selected polymers; no general concentration reported hereFTIR; {{claim:s-d2f3af1338e5-size-window}}Positive negative controls and operating-room materials complicate interpretation

The clinical pilot detected polyethylene, polypropylene and polyurethane in initial placental screening and polyethylene in an initial meconium sample. Some negative controls were positive as well. After modifying sampling, the investigators found polypropylene in a placental core and polypropylene and polystyrene in meconium, while another placental control contained polystyrene and operating-room fallout contained polyurethane. The detailed pattern matters more than a single headline that tissue “contained plastic.”{{cite:s-d2f3af1338e5}}

How contamination was evaluated

The clinical investigators examined surgical materials, collection instruments, storage containers and airborne fallout alongside biological specimens. They also used dedicated cleanroom handling and procedural blanks. These checks revealed potential contamination that would have been missed by analyzing only the tissue. They strengthen the paper as a methods lesson, while limiting the extent to which any isolated positive finding can be attributed to material present before clinical collection.{{cite:s-d2f3af1338e5}}

The olfactory-bulb investigators minimized plastic contact and used blanks throughout processing. They compared spectra with polymer libraries, including weathered plastic reference material. Biological tissue can nonetheless interfere with spectral interpretation. The authors reported that a recovery test was not feasible, and digested tissue was unavailable for some cases. The microscope's resolution did not permit nanoplastic detection. A pore size used during filtration therefore should not be presented as the validated size of every particle the complete method could detect.{{cite:s-d78cd56bfc44}}

What remains unresolved

Detecting particles in an olfactory bulb does not identify a demonstrated entry route. The authors discussed the olfactory pathway but acknowledged that other routes could not be excluded. A cross-sectional postmortem observation cannot show when an object entered the tissue, how long it remained or whether it contributed to a neurological condition. The occurrence fraction describes the studied decedents; it is not a population prevalence estimate.{{cite:s-d78cd56bfc44}}

Likewise, screening placenta or meconium is not evidence of a quantified fetal dose or a measured developmental outcome. Contamination controls, the small pilot design and the specified size and polymer window all constrain interpretation. These studies motivate careful measurement, but they cannot identify a safer consumer product or support a health claim about an untested item.{{cite:s-d2f3af1338e5}}

Results should retain their original measurement basis. A count of objects, a positive chemical identification and a polymer mass concentration are different quantities. No conversion among them is made here. The most useful reading of human biomonitoring pairs the reported finding with its tissue, analytical method, size capability and controls, while keeping source attribution and causal health conclusions open unless directly studied.{{cite:s-d2f3af1338e5}}{{cite:s-d78cd56bfc44}}

Regulatory status

The supplied regulatory-method documents do not provide a clinical diagnostic cutoff for particles in human tissue. The California framework explicitly distinguishes a monitoring-screening approach from an established human-health threshold; its workshop evidence is not a clinical test standard.{{cite:s-a3ddbf43f296}} Drinking-water methods cannot be transferred to tissue or air without matrix-specific validation.{{cite:s-b8033a33708a}} Read regulatory and analytical scope.

title: Microplastics released from textiles
scope: Laundry, polyester fibers and controlled abrasion
description: Primary textile experiments on released fiber mass, particle counts, fine fibrils and nanoparticles.
body:
Washing and abrasion experiments have measured plastic fibers released from selected synthetic textiles. Release depends on the fabric construction, laundering conditions and particle fraction measured. The results below describe release to test liquid or laundry wastewater. They do not directly measure how many particles a person inhales or absorbs while wearing clothing.{{cite:s-ec050c3d5049}}{{cite:s-1cab99d72043}}

Which textiles and processes were tested

The reviewed experiments include household-machine washing of commercial garments and a controlled polyester-fleece study that compared washing with abrasion followed by washing. They cover specific materials and laboratory conditions rather than the full range of apparel and outdoor gear. A result from fleece should not be assigned to a coated shell, tent, shoe or other untested product.{{cite:s-ec050c3d5049}}{{cite:s-1cab99d72043}}

Textile fibers also require a material distinction. Synthetic polymer fibers can be microplastics, while cotton, modal and other cellulosic fibers should not automatically be counted as plastic. One household-laundry paper included a mixed garment that shed substantial cellulose. This page keeps its pure-polyester garment results separate from that mixed-fiber total, instead of calling every released fiber microplastic.{{cite:s-ec050c3d5049}}

What the experiments found

The household washing study measured {{claim:s-ec050c3d5049-polyester-knit}} from a tested knitted garment and {{claim:s-ec050c3d5049-polyester-woven}} from a tested woven garment in the first wash. The quantities are fiber mass normalized to washed fabric mass. The garments differed in construction and yarn properties, so the comparison does not isolate the effect of a single design variable or establish a ranking for all knitted and woven textiles.{{cite:s-ec050c3d5049}}

Scroll horizontally for methods and limits.

Study and materialReported resultMethod and size contextLimit
Pure-polyester knitted garment, first household wash{{cite:s-ec050c3d5049}}{{claim:s-ec050c3d5049-polyester-knit}}Whole-effluent staged filtration, gravimetry and FTIRSelected garment and duplicate trials; mass is not a direct count
Pure-polyester woven garment, first household wash{{cite:s-ec050c3d5049}}{{claim:s-ec050c3d5049-polyester-woven}}Same household-washing workflowFabric structure and recycled content were not independently varied
Polyester fleece, controlled wash{{cite:s-1cab99d72043}}{{claim:s-1cab99d72043-wash-fibers}}SEM count of conventional microplastic fibersTested fleece; method-blank contribution subtracted
Same fleece after abrasion followed by washing{{cite:s-1cab99d72043}}{{claim:s-1cab99d72043-abraded-fibers}}SEM; fine fibrils classified separatelyLiquid extraction result, not measured airborne shedding
Polyester fleece, nanoparticle fraction of wash liquid{{cite:s-1cab99d72043}}{{claim:s-1cab99d72043-wash-nano}}NTA counting; {{claim:s-1cab99d72043-nano-window}}; PET chemistry supported in selected particlesNTA is not particle-by-particle polymer identification; substantial blank background

The fleece study distinguished ordinary cylindrical microfibers from narrower tape-like fibrils. Fibrils were found after abrasion, while conventional fibers were counted in both conditions. It also detected PET nanoparticles using chemical analysis of selected particles. This combination shows that focusing only on visible fibers can omit other fractions, but it does not make every nanoparticle counted by a physical instrument a separately confirmed polymer particle.{{cite:s-1cab99d72043}}

Mass, counts and chemical identity

The household study collected the complete wastewater volume through staged filters and weighed the recovered fibers. It also published estimated fiber numbers calculated from mass, mean dimensions, density and an assumed cylindrical shape. Those estimates are not direct counts and are not reproduced as independently measured particle totals here. A smaller filter was used on an aliquot to demonstrate a fine fraction; the authors did not extrapolate that aliquot to the entire wastewater volume.{{cite:s-ec050c3d5049}}

In the fleece experiment, SEM image analysis counted microfibers and fibrils. Nanoparticle tracking analysis estimated number and size from physical particle motion. Transmission electron microscopy examined morphology, while scanning transmission X-ray microscopy and absorption spectra supported PET identity in selected nanoparticles. The reported nanoparticle abundance used {{claim:s-1cab99d72043-nano-window}}. Smaller observed objects were excluded from that quantitative window rather than assumed to have a confirmed plastic identity.{{cite:s-1cab99d72043}}

Both studies assessed background contamination. The household-machine work used cleaning cycles and blank tests without detected fibers. The controlled fleece work processed method blanks through the same washing, filtration and centrifugation steps and subtracted background. The latter included a substantial nanoparticle background, which is particularly relevant when interpreting very large number concentrations. Chemical confirmation of selected particles and blank subtraction strengthen interpretation but do not remove every analytical assumption.{{cite:s-ec050c3d5049}}{{cite:s-1cab99d72043}}

What the results mean for product evidence

These experiments establish release under their stated conditions. They do not show the total emitted over a garment's lifetime or the portion reaching a person. Laundering intensity, textile preparation, abrasion and sample collection differ between the papers, so the quantities cannot be pooled into a universal shedding factor. Fiber mass and nanoparticle counts also cannot be compared as if they were the same measurement.{{cite:s-ec050c3d5049}}{{cite:s-1cab99d72043}}

The studies support further work on fabric structure and testing methods, while leaving important product-specific gaps. Neither a polymer label nor a recycled-content label alone determines release. The household study explicitly noted that construction differences prevented isolating recycled content as the explanation for its results. No brand comparison, wearer health claim or untested outdoor-gear estimate follows from these experiments.{{cite:s-ec050c3d5049}}{{cite:s-1cab99d72043}}

Regulatory status

The supplied EU restriction addresses defined synthetic polymer microparticles as substances or intentionally present in mixtures, with exclusions, derogations and transition provisions. A shedding measurement from an article does not by itself establish whether that restriction applies or has been violated.{{cite:s-2f1daf6ca78b}} The drinking-water methods are useful analytical comparisons, but they are not validated product-specific release tests for this category.{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}} No universal compliant particle count is inferred from them. Read the regulatory source guide.

title: How microplastics are measured
scope: Analytical interpretation
description: Why polymer identification, particle size, measurement units, sample preparation, and controls matter when comparing studies.
body:
Match the method to the result

Raman and FTIR can provide chemical information about polymer material. Microscopy also records particle appearance or size, but fluorescent or visible objects need an identification workflow before they can be treated as chemically identified plastic particles. {{cite:cella-2022-food-packaging-methods}}{{cite:ajaj-2021-polystyrene-packaging}}

Nile Red staining and confocal imaging supplied counts in the food-wrap study, while characterization of the bulk film was performed separately. Keep that distinction visible rather than calling the counted objects individually Raman-confirmed. {{cite:wang-2024-ldpe-food-wrap}}

Keep counts and mass separate

A polymer-mass result cannot be converted to a particle count without information about the particles. Area-normalized counts, counts per container, and chemical concentrations answer different questions. The source studies retain those denominators. {{cite:cella-2022-food-packaging-methods}}{{cite:wang-2024-ldpe-food-wrap}}{{cite:wang-2023-polystyrene-containers}}

Read the controls and size window

Check how laboratory contamination was controlled, whether blanks were processed, which particles were retained, and how polymer identity was established. Sample preparation and aggregation can affect what is counted. A filter’s pore size is not automatically a validated analytical detection limit. {{cite:cella-2022-food-packaging-methods}}

What remains uncertain

These method descriptions explain the reviewed studies. They do not establish a universal food-storage test or make results from unlike methods interchangeable.

What the supplied water methods add

The California IR procedure states a lowest reliably detected size of {{claim:s-2f979a7f686b-lower-size}}; the Raman procedure states {{claim:s-5a6c89659a69-lower-size}}. Both apply to treated drinking water within their specified procedures. These values do not describe all FTIR or Raman instruments and do not establish a nanoplastic detection capability.{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}}

The EU water decision combines morphology or chemical mapping with polymer identification. It distinguishes particle-number measurements from mass-only thermal measurements. JRC practical guidance explains why blanks, recovery, sizing and reporting are essential, and why extension to another matrix requires evaluation.{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}}{{cite:s-b8033a33708a}}

title: Regulatory and agency context
scope: EU instruments and California water methods
description: Legal instruments, official water methods, technical reports, and scientific assessments, with their scopes and versions kept distinct.
body:
Read each document within its authority and scope

The regulatory-method library contains legal instruments, official laboratory methods, policy material, technical reports and scientific assessments. They answer different questions. A legal restriction on an intentional ingredient, a procedure for counting particles in drinking water, and a laboratory finding in food are not interchangeable.

SourceWhat it establishesWhat is not inferred
EU synthetic polymer microparticle restriction{{cite:s-2f1daf6ca78b}}Defined substance/mixture restriction, with exclusions, derogations and transitionsA blanket ban on plastic articles or every particle shed from them
EU drinking-water decision{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}}A methodology combining collection, morphology and polymer identificationA health-based particle ceiling or universal food/product release test
California IR and Raman procedures{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}}Treated-water analytical methods with stated size coverage and quality controlsAutomatic validation for food, air, dust or tissue
Supplied California handbook{{cite:s-f4ab6cdc2d0b}}Monitoring-policy context in the supplied pre-adoption versionA verified present-day implementation timetable
JRC technical reports{{cite:s-324980b0826d}}{{cite:s-b8033a33708a}}Analytical evaluation and practical method guidanceA separate legal concentration limit
EFSA statement and California research framework{{cite:s-aa0dd4c46340}}{{cite:s-a3ddbf43f296}}Dated scientific assessment and monitoring-framework evidenceA product-specific safe particle count or clinical diagnostic threshold

Versions and current-source checks

The California handbook supplied in the library carries an August 9, 2022 cover date. The current agency microplastics index, checked on the page update date, separately lists adoption under Resolution 2022-0032 and the revised laboratory methods. The library identifies the supplied version rather than treating proposed dates as verified implementation. The methods themselves are the supplied revised versions.{{cite:s-f4ab6cdc2d0b}}{{cite:s-2f979a7f686b}}{{cite:s-5a6c89659a69}}

The EU decision adopts its methodology in Article 1 and addresses Member States in Article 2. A particular water product must be considered within the scope of the parent drinking-water directive; this page does not assume that every bottled-water study is a public-water compliance test.{{cite:s-f59f482c1c39}}

Food-contact and scientific context

FDA describes a food-contact authorization framework using intended use, migration and toxicological evidence, alongside important analytical gaps for microplastics.{{cite:fda-microplastics-foods}} The supplied EFSA food/seafood statement is a dated scientific assessment. Its historical description of legislation is not repeated as a claim about all current laws.{{cite:s-aa0dd4c46340}}

Monitoring is distinct from a safe level

The California research framework could develop a conservative monitoring-screening approach, but could not extrapolate an established human-health threshold. A screening calculation is not an observed product concentration or a clinical cutoff.{{cite:s-a3ddbf43f296}}

This is a bounded source guide, not a worldwide legal register. The category pages apply only the context their cited documents support.

title: Editorial and evidence approach
scope: How this collection is compiled
description: Source identity, exact reported values, study-specific interpretation, and transparent evidence gaps.
body:
Keep every finding traceable

The library checks source identity and preserves the original artifact hash alongside extracted findings. Published measurements retain their units, denominator, material, conditions, method, size context, and location in the paper.

Keep the boundaries visible

A missing value is omitted. A chemical concentration is not a particle count. A laboratory release experiment is not a measured human dose or a clinical outcome. Results from unlike studies remain separate.

Coverage

The collection follows the supplied category library. Every supplied PDF was inventoried, hash-checked and screened for topic relevance. Selected original papers were examined in their methods and results; reviews, misfiled papers and candidates not deeply reviewed are recorded separately. Category pages are selected literature syntheses, not exhaustive systematic reviews. A folder containing only a review cannot supply an invented product measurement.
